c.tagline: Neon harbor nights and dim-sum mornings.

avoid.reason: Very safe; usual pickpocket caution; avoid protests (national-security law risks)

hood_desc: The dense financial heart of the city, packed with skyscrapers, luxury malls, and buzzing after-work bars around Lan Kwai Fong; ideal for business travelers and nightlife seekers who want to be in the thick of it.
A tourist-friendly Kowloon waterfront district famous for the Avenue of Stars, harbor skyline views, museums, and endless shopping, suiting first-time visitors and sightseers.
A frenetic shopping and dining hub with department stores, boutiques, and crowded streets, popular with young shoppers and foodies looking for a lively urban buzz.
One of the most densely populated places on earth, this gritty, energetic Kowloon area is full of street markets, cheap eats, and neon, great for budget travelers and market lovers.
A mixed business-and-nightlife district with old wet markets alongside trendy bars, restaurants, and the convention center, appealing to both professionals and revelers.

water.note: Meets world-class standards; safe in modern buildings, though older plumbing means some flush taps briefly first.

transit.pay: Get an Octopus card — it works on the MTR, trams, ferries and buses. Buy one at airport or MTR customer service counters (about HK$50 deposit, ~US$6.50) or add it to Apple/Google Wallet. Contactless Visa and Mastercard are now also accepted directly at MTR fare gates.
transit.hours: MTR runs roughly 6am to 1am daily. Overnight, N-prefixed night buses and taxis cover the gaps.

food.name: Dim sum
food.desc: Cantonese small plates - har gow, siu mai and baked char siu buns - shared over morning tea, Hong Kong's defining meal.

places.name: Tim Ho Wan
places.note: World's cheapest Michelin-starred meal; baked BBQ pork buns still draw queues per 2025 guides

places.name: One Dim Sum
places.note: Former Michelin-listed bargain spot locals rate alongside Tim Ho Wan

places.name: Luk Yu Tea House
places.note: 1933 teahouse praised in 2025 roundups for old-world trolley-era atmosphere

food.name: Roast goose
food.desc: Crackling lacquered skin over juicy meat, chopped to order and served on rice or noodles - the king of Cantonese roast meats.

places.name: Yat Lok
places.note: One Michelin star; repeatedly named Hong Kong's best goose in 2024-2025 comparisons

places.name: Kam's Roast Goose
places.note: Michelin-starred heir to the 70-year Yung Kee goose dynasty; cleaner, less greasy style

food.name: Wonton noodle soup
food.desc: Springy egg noodles and shrimp-packed wontons in a light dried-flounder broth, eaten in minutes at old-school shops.

places.name: Mak's Noodle
places.note: The famous Mak family original, still open daily and a fixture of tourism-board food guides

places.name: Ho Hung Kee
places.note: Michelin-recognized 1946 noodle house inside Hysan Place

places.name: Tsim Chai Kee
places.note: Locals' value pick across the street from Mak's; giant wontons, short queue turnover

food.name: Egg tart
food.desc: Buttery cookie-crust tart with wobbling golden custard, best eaten warm from the oven.

places.name: Tai Cheong Bakery
places.note: 1954 institution famed for its shortcrust tarts; constant 2024-2025 best-of listings

places.name: Bakehouse
places.note: Gregoire Michaud's sourdough egg tart is the city's biggest modern queue per recent reviews

food.name: Egg waffle (gai daan zai)
food.desc: Bubbly griddled waffle, crisp outside and custardy inside - Hong Kong's favorite street snack since the 1950s.

places.name: Mammy Pancake
places.note: Michelin street-food listed; classic and creative flavors, several branches

places.name: Lee Keung Kee North Point Egg Waffles
places.note: Decades-old stall many locals call the benchmark bubble waffle

food.name: Pineapple bun with butter (bolo yau)
food.desc: Warm sugar-crusted bun split around a cold slab of butter - the classic cha chaan teng treat with milk tea.

places.name: Kam Wah Cafe
places.note: The city's most famous bolo bao, baked fresh all day; a staple of 2025 food guides

places.name: Kam Fung Cafe
places.note: Old-school 1950s cafe beloved for pineapple buns and chicken pies

food.name: Hong Kong milk tea
food.desc: Strong black tea pulled through a 'silk stocking' filter and smoothed with evaporated milk - the city's daily fuel.

places.name: Lan Fong Yuen
places.note: 1952 dai pai dong credited with inventing silk-stocking milk tea; still queues daily

places.name: Capital Cafe
places.note: Retro cha chaan teng praised in recent guides for silky milk tea and scrambled-egg toast

food.name: Local craft beer
food.desc: Hong Kong's craft scene, led by Young Master, pours salted-lime gose and city-inspired ales in lively taprooms.

places.name: Young Master Brewery Taproom
places.note: The territory's flagship craft brewery; weekend taproom tours and fresh pours

places.name: Second Draft
places.note: Gastropub with rotating local taps and Cantonese bar food, a fixture of Time Out lists

landmarks: Victoria Peak
Hong Kong's highest point delivers the definitive skyscraper-and-harbour skyline view, especially at dusk.
Star Ferry (Tsim Sha Tsui)
The century-old green-and-white ferry crossing Victoria Harbour is a nostalgic, endlessly photogenic Hong Kong icon.
Hong Kong Disneyland
A fairy-tale castle park on Lantau Island, popular for its classic Disney-castle photo backdrop.
Ngong Ping 360 / Tian Tan Buddha
A cable car ride up to the giant bronze Big Buddha on Lantau Island, striking against mountain backdrops.
A Symphony of Lights (Victoria Harbour)
A nightly multimedia light show synchronized across the harbourfront skyscrapers, best captured after sunset.
Repulse Bay
A scenic sandy beach ringed by high-rise towers, a favorite for contrast shots of nature against the skyline.
Man Mo Temple
A historic incense-filled Taoist temple in Sheung Wan, famous for its dramatic hanging incense coils.
Choi Hung Estate
A rainbow-colored public housing estate with a basketball court, one of the most Instagrammed spots in the city.
International Commerce Centre (ICC)
Hong Kong's tallest skyscraper, home to the sky100 observation deck with unrivaled city views.
Central, Hong Kong Island skyline
The dense cluster of skyscrapers in Central forms the quintessential Hong Kong skyline photograph.

intl.to: Beijing & other mainland cities (day high-speed trains)

dom.op: MTR (urban metro and local lines only)

train.note: All cross-border trains leave from Hong Kong West Kowloon station; crossing into mainland China is a full border crossing, so bring your passport (and a Chinese visa if you need one) and allow time for immigration. The overnight high-speed sleepers to Beijing and Shanghai run on selected days — check dates when booking.

intl.to: Zhuhai & Macau via the HZMB bridge

bus.note: The HZMB shuttle ('Golden Bus') runs around the clock from the HZMB Hong Kong Port near the airport; you clear immigration on foot and hop on the next bus. Eternal East also runs cross-border coaches to Guangdong. Passport (and mainland visa if required) needed for all routes.

intl.to: Zhuhai & other Pearl River Delta ports (mainland China)

ferry.note: Ferries sail from the Hong Kong–Macau Ferry Terminal at Sheung Wan and the China Ferry Terminal in Tsim Sha Tsui; crossings to Macau take about an hour. TurboJET also serves Zhuhai, and SkyPier ferries at the airport are for connecting air passengers only.

half.name: Lantau Island
half.blurb: Home to the giant Tian Tan Big Buddha, a scenic cable car and the old fishing village of Tai O.

half.name: Macau
half.blurb: People go for its glittering casinos, Portuguese colonial streets and famous egg tarts across the delta.

half.name: Cheung Chau
half.blurb: A laid-back car-free island loved for seafood, beaches, temples and its lively annual bun festival.

half.name: Lamma Island
half.blurb: A relaxed green island known for easy hiking trails, sandy coves and waterfront seafood restaurants.

half.name: Sai Kung
half.blurb: A seaside town and gateway to the Geopark's dramatic coastline, boat trips and quiet beaches.

half.name: Shenzhen
half.blurb: Just across the border, people cross for its shopping malls, theme parks and buzzing city energy.
